narrative: The model estimates a 58% probability that you will leave, so it judges you slightly more likely than not to depart. Because the promotion decision treats that as a retention risk, you were denied. The three most important factors, in order, all pushed toward leaving. First, you have received other job opportunities; only about 23% of employees predicted to stay had such offers, so this was the strongest signal of mobility. Second, your total experience is 11+ years; only about 15% of stayers have that much experience, which the model associates with greater likelihood of leaving. Third, you report difficult work-life balance; only about 9% of stayers did, so this also increased the leave prediction. The organization should treat this as a prompt for a retention conversation, not a final judgment. It should review promotion criteria, workload, flexibility and career pathways. You should ask for specific feedback, discuss the opportunities you have and your work-life constraints, and agree on a development or retention plan. If you intend to stay, say so clearly and ask what would need to change for the promotion decision to be reconsidered.
